summary: Describes how the MIT Lincoln Laboratory IBM 360/67 let other ARPANET users log in and use it. After logging in, a user got a whole virtual 360 machine with a virtual console, card reader, printer and disks. The document is a description of one site's service rather than a general standard.

eli5.summary: One big computer pretends to be many small computers, one for each visitor. This note explains how a faraway visitor could knock on the door and get their own pretend computer.

subtitle: How the Lincoln Laboratory IBM 360/67 let ARPANET users log in and get their own virtual 360.

tldr.problem: Network users needed a documented way to reach the Lincoln Laboratory IBM 360/67, which runs the CP-67 virtual machine operating system.
tldr.mechanism: A user makes a pair of connections to the LOGGER through the Initial Connection Protocol, chooses ASCII or EBCDIC, and logs in. A SERVER then relays lines between the network and CP-67.
tldr.outcome: After login the user controls a virtual 360 with a virtual console, card reader, card punch, printer and disks. This is one site's service description, not a general standard.

today: The metadata gives this RFC an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a single 1971 host's service, not a general protocol.

sections.title: The Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 Host
sections.content:
The IBM 360/67 at Lincoln Laboratory is connected to the ARPA network and acts as a serving host giving access to the CP-67 virtual machine operating system. After Login, users control a 360 virtual machine through a virtual 1052 online console, with a virtual card reader, card punch, line printer and a number of disks.

The virtual machine can be a 360/67 with dynamic address translation or a standard System/360. Most users run a standard 360 with 256K bytes of virtual memory and the CMS conversational monitor system. All network communication goes through a Network Control Program using the Host-Host Protocol of Document No. 1, dated 3 August 1970. The RFC carries a disclaimer that it should not be quoted outside ARPA network use.
sections.eli5: Visitors from the network get their own pretend computer inside the big one, with a pretend screen, card reader and printer.

sections.title: Connecting and Logging In
sections.content:
To create a virtual machine, a pair of connections is made with the LOGGER using the Initial Connection Protocol. The LOGGER waits for an RTS on the ICP socket X'0A 0000 01'. If it will serve another user, it sends a 32-bit receive socket ID over this connection and the ICP socket is closed. If not, it refuses by closing the connection without completing it.

The LOGGER then expects one 8-bit byte giving the data type: X'01' means 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit bytes and X'02' means 8-bit EBCDIC. It echoes the code and sends LINCOLN LABORATORY CP-67 ONLINE, then login follows the normal CP-67 procedure. The LOGGER maps network userids and passwords to valid CP-67 ones using the LOGGER FILE, so only accounts with an entry can be reached. One account, userid NET, is offered for trying the system, with 900 records of storage, and users may erase any of its files.
sections.eli5: You knock on a special door, say whether you speak ASCII or EBCDIC, and a doorman checks your name and password against a list.

sections.title: The Server: Lines, Prompts and Interrupts
sections.content:
CP-67 works a line at a time, and input is not normally entered until the system asks for it. When CP requests a line, the SERVER sends the prompting code X'80'. Characters received are buffered until an NL arrives, and CP may send lines that do or do not end in NL.

To interrupt a CP process, the user sends the interrupt code X'80', which acts like pressing the 'attention' button on a 2741 terminal. An INS is sent over the send link at the same time and is paired with the interrupt code; characters buffered before the code arrives are flushed. If CP has output before it received any input, the SERVER sends an INS on the receive link so the user retracts the prompt, and the line is called a 'warning'.
sections.eli5: The computer says 'your turn' with a special signal, and you can tap a special signal of your own to get its attention.

sections.title: Character Codes
sections.content:
The RFC closes with figures giving the 8-bit EBCDIC and 7-bit ASCII graphics and controls, a comparison of the controls, and the standard meanings of the ASCII controls. Four ASCII codes have no EBCDIC counterpart and are assigned EBCDIC codes: DC3 (13 to 3A), ` (60 to 70), \ (5C to 71) and ^ (5E to 72).

CP-67 sends BYP (Bypass) around password entry to suspend printing and RES (Restore) afterwards. In ASCII these are converted to X'FF' because no ASCII code matches.
sections.eli5: Two computers can write letters with different secret codes, so this note includes a translation table between the two.
